raw_case_text:
The patient was born in Realeza, Parana State, Brazil, and his family moved to Corpus Christi, Paraguay, when he was 9 years old, where he stayed for about 10 years. Then, he returned to Brazil, residing in Sete Quedas, Mato Grosso do Sul State, Marcelandia, Mato Grosso State, and Ribeirao Preto, Sao Paulo State, several years in each of these municipalities. He has worked for a long time as a truck and tractor driver, transporting manioc and wood, and has lived in a rural area, close to a deforestation area. He had contact with sawmills and prolonged exposure to wood dust. The patient claimed to be a heavy smoker since his youth and that he is used to drinking from 50 mL to 1 L of distilled alcoholic beverages per day. He has also reported a cutaneous leishmaniasis 16 years earlier.
Blood count and blood biochemical tests were normal, except for a high C-reactive protein (12.3 mg/dL). Serological tests for HIV infection, leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, and hepatitis C virus were negative, but serum anti-HBc Ag IgG antibodies were detected. Serological screening for systemic mycoses by the counterimmunoelectrophoresis (CIE) method was negative for histoplasmosis and aspergillosis, but positive for paracoccidioidomycosis with a 1:8 titer against P. brasiliensis antigen.
A chest X-ray showed diffuse infiltrates in both lungs, especially in the perihilar region, with a reticular and micronodular appearance and areas of alveolar opacities. The investigation through computed tomography (CT) showed that both adrenals were enlarged and had hypodense areas. Plasma cortisol (7.8 mug/dL) was just above the lowest level of the normal range (5.0 mug/dL). The histopathological examination of a skin lesion collected by biopsy showed granulomatous inflammatory infiltrateswith giant cells and yeasts presenting with exosporulation. The culture of the biopsied skin lesion led to the isolation of Paracoccidioides spp.
The patient was diagnosed with the chronic form of paracoccidioidomycosis, presenting with lung, skin and adrenal lesions. The antifungal treatment was carried out with itraconazole (400 mg/day), leading to a progressive improvement, except for the appearance of dyspnea during intense physical activities . About 40 days after the beginning of the treatment, the patient had accentuated dyspnea, dry coughand worsening of his physical condition. The skin lesions were healed, but there were crepitations in both lungs, a respiratory rate of 36/min, and arterial O2 saturation between 87% and 92%. No clinical signs of heart failure were detected and echocardiography was not perfomed at this time. The radiological pattern of the lungs had worsened ( Figure 2 ). Trimethoprim:sulfamethoxazole, at a dose of 160 mg of trimethoprim was introduced intravenously every 8 h and prednisone was associated at a dose of 20 mg/day, orally. The dyspnea decreased and treatment with itraconazole was reintroduced after 5 days in association with the corticosteroid therapy, maintained for 50 days.
After four months of antifungal therapy, pulmonary vital capacity and airway flow were normal in the spirometry evaluation. A chest CT scan showed thickened bronchi walls, some with dilation, lungs with a diffuse pattern that looked like micronodules, ground-glass opacities and cardiomegaly ( Figure 2 ). Histological examination of tissues obtained by bronchoscopy revealed lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates associated with bronchial and vascular remodeling, aside from distortion of the tissue architecture ( Figure 3 ). Doppler echocardiography showed slight dilation of the left atrium, ascending aorta and pulmonary artery, in addition to pulmonary arterial hypertension (pulmonary artery systolic pressure estimated at 42 mmHg, normal limit < 25 mmHg). The performed tests led to the conclusion that the patient had sequelae of paracoccidioidomycosis, functional changes in the lung and pulmonary circulation. The dose of itraconazole was reduced to 200 mg/day, completing the 17 months of antifungal use.
In the clinical follow up, the patient maintained dyspnea of varied intensities. A new chest CT scan performed eight months after the end of treatment showed a decrease in pulmonary opacities, the presence of bronchiectasis, a slight increase in the right ventricle and dilation of the pulmonary artery trunk (32 mm, normal range: < 29 mm).
Total genomic DNA of Paracoccidioides spp. isolated from the patient's lesions was extracted and ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 rDNA, as well as gp43 exon 2 gene regions were amplified by PCR, purified and sequenced. Gene sequencing was carried out on the platform of the Human Genome and Stem-Cell Research Center, Institute of Biosciences of the University of Sao Paulo. The comparison of the Pb 01 ( P. lutzii ) nucleotide sequences revealed similarities of 99.5% with the ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 rDNA sequence (accession N  EU870297.1) and 100% with the gp43 exon 2 loci sequence (accession N  EU870196.1). The fungus isolated from the patient was therefore identified as P. lutzii and the obtained gene sequences (ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 rDNA and gp43 exon 2) were deposited in GenBank (accession N  MK909806 and MK886790, respectively) .

subjective.chief_complaint: A male truck and tractor driver with a history of rural deforestation and wood-dust exposure in Brazil and Paraguay presented with skin, pulmonary, and bilateral adrenal lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with cutaneous, pulmonary, and adrenal involvement; 40 days after initiating oral itraconazole (400 mg/day) with healing of skin lesions, he developed worsening exertional and resting dyspnea and a dry cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cutaneous leishmaniasis 16 years earlier. Epidemiological/social history: Born in Parana State, Brazil, lived in Paraguay for 10 years, and worked in rural Mato Grosso do Sul, Mato Grosso, and Sao Paulo States as a manioc/wood truck and tractor driver near deforestation areas and sawmills with prolonged wood-dust exposure; heavy lifelong smoker and consumed 50 mL to 1 L of distilled alcohol daily.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for skin lesions, progressive exertional dyspnea, and dry cough.

objective.physical_examination: At day 40 exacerbation: healed skin lesions, bilateral pulmonary crepitations, RR 36/min, SpO2 87-92%, and no clinical signs of heart failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs: normal CBC and blood chemistry except elevated CRP (12.3 mg/dL); plasma cortisol 7.8 ug/dL (lower limit of normal 5.0 ug/dL); negative HIV, leishmaniasis, Chagas, and HCV serologies; positive anti-HBc IgG. Counterimmunoelectrophoresis (CIE) fungal serology: negative for histoplasmosis and aspergillosis; positive for paracoccidioidomycosis (1:8 titer). Chest X-ray: diffuse bilateral perihilar reticular, micronodular, and alveolar infiltrates. Spirometry (at 4 months): normal vital capacity and airflow. Doppler echocardiography: mild dilation of LA, ascending aorta, and pulmonary artery (32 mm) with pulmonary arterial hypertension (estimated PASP 42 mmHg, normal <25 mmHg).
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT: bilateral adrenal enlargement with hypodense areas. Serial chest CTs: thickened dilated bronchial walls, bronchiectasis, diffuse micronodular and ground-glass opacities, cardiomegaly, mild RV enlargement, and pulmonary artery trunk dilation. Bronchoscopy biopsy (at 4 months): lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with bronchial and vascular remodeling. Skin lesion biopsy, culture, and PCR sequencing (ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 rDNA and gp43 exon 2): granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and exosporulating yeasts; culture and sequencing confirmed Paracoccidioides lutzii (GenBank MK909806 and MK886790).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Chronic multifocal Paracoccidioides lutzii infection (lung, skin, and adrenal involvement) complicated by post-treatment pulmonary fibrosis, bronchiectasis, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (histoplasmosis and aspergillosis ruled out by negative CIE serology). Confirmation: Skin biopsy histopathology showing exosporulating yeasts, positive CIE titer (1:8), fungal culture isolation, and PCR/sequencing of ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 and gp43 exon 2 confirming Paracoccidioides lutzii. Plan & clinical course: Treated with oral itraconazole (400 mg/day, reduced to 200 mg/day to complete 17 months total), with a 50-day course of oral prednisone (20 mg/day) and 5 days of IV TMP-SMX added at day 40 for paradoxical/inflammatory pulmonary worsening; skin lesions resolved, while residual dyspnea, bronchiectasis, and mild pulmonary hypertension persisted on follow-up.
